# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Finds Its Way Up

Water is heavy. A single cubic foot of it weighs about 62 pounds, and a gallon tips the scale at over eight pounds. This simple fact governs everything about how a municipal water system works, because moving water upward—against gravity—is the central engineering challenge of delivering it to a tenth-floor apartment. The remarkable thing is that most of the system does this without any moving parts at all, exploiting physics rather than fighting it.

## The Fundamental Principle: Elevation as Energy

Water systems run on a concept engineers call "head," which is essentially stored energy expressed in feet of elevation. Water at a height of 100 feet has 100 feet of head, and every 2.31 feet of elevation corresponds to roughly one pound per square inch (psi) of pressure. This means that if a reservoir sits 200 feet above your kitchen faucet, the water arriving at that faucet will emerge at about 86 psi, minus losses along the way—no pump required.
